core.title: Assert on the returned markup fragment, not just the status
core.given: In a test within a markup-fragment hypermedia stack (a stack-level membership fact: the application serves markup fragments; not a per-endpoint response-contract test), a test case performs an actual HTTP request against the served application (not a direct unit call of the boundary handler) and asserts on the response status or success flag
core.when: the tester writes or changes that test case
core.then: The test case MUST also assert on the response body; reaching the body in any form — reading it, parsing it, or asserting on its content with a markup/content matcher — satisfies the rule.
prefer: Assert on the returned fragment, not just the status line: keep the status assertion, then reach the body and assert on the markup it returns — for example on the element id that a later fragment swap targets.

When the response is a markup fragment, make the body assertion check the fragment contract — the declarative markup attributes, the element ids later swaps (including out-of-band swaps) target, and the structure — as in the reference example.
avoid: Status-only tests: asserting on the response status or success flag and stopping — proves the route exists and nothing about what the user will see.
unless: The case does not perform an HTTP request (out of scope).
The case never asserts on status (out of scope). Note: asserting on the response's success flag counts as a status assertion, so a success-flag-only case is in scope.
core.why: In a payload API the contract is the payload, and status plus a parsed field is a complete test; in a hypermedia stack the contract is the markup (the declarative attributes, the element ids later swaps target, the structure) swapped into the live DOM. A status-only test misses a refactor dropping an id that a sibling fragment's out-of-band swap needs, which fails silently at runtime.
evidence: Every in-scope test case that performs an HTTP request and asserts on status or the success flag also reaches the body by reading it, parsing it, or a markup/content matcher.
The stack's tester-discipline check reports zero findings for the changed test files.
verification: Flag a test case that performs an actual HTTP request, asserts on the response status or success flag, and never reaches the response body (by reading it, parsing it, or asserting on its content).
Reaching the body in any form — reading it, parsing it, or a content/markup matcher on the returned markup — satisfies the rule.

Skip test cases that perform no HTTP request, including direct unit calls of a boundary handler that return a response object; skip cases that never assert on status (a success-flag assertion counts as a status assertion).
Severity 3; disposition strict: the check fails on every finding; there is no advisory mode and no ratchet baseline.

Scope: only test files of stacks that realize this rule (paradigmatically, markup-fragment hypermedia stacks) — a stack-level membership fact determined by the realization, not a per-endpoint response-contract test. Within an in-scope stack, the check covers every test case that performs an HTTP request and asserts on status or the success flag, regardless of the individual endpoint's response contract; no payload-endpoint exclusion is added.

fires: In a hypermedia-stack test file, a test case performs an HTTP request against the served application, asserts on the response status, and ends without reaching the body.
In a hypermedia-stack test file, a test case performs an HTTP request and asserts only on the response's success flag, with no body read, parse, or markup/content assertion on the response.
doesNotFire: A test case that performs no HTTP request, including a direct unit call of a boundary handler that returns a response object and asserts its status.
A test case that performs an HTTP request but never asserts on status or the success flag.
A test case that asserts on status or the success flag and also reaches the body by reading it, parsing it, or a markup/content matcher.
Test suites outside the realizing markup-fragment stack (this rule has no counterpart in the tester extensions of other stacks) — a stack-level exclusion, not a per-endpoint one.

neutralityNotes: Round-2 fixes: (1) Scope is now purely stack-level, matching bun.json's Bun/htmx stack-membership scoping. A stack is in scope when it realizes this rule (paradigmatically, a markup-fragment hypermedia stack); within an in-scope stack the check covers every test case that performs an HTTP request and asserts on status or the success flag, regardless of the individual endpoint's response contract — the previous per-endpoint markup requirement (in fires) and payload-API exclusion (in verification) are removed. (2) idiom.markup_kinds is no longer referenced: its documented meaning is artifact kinds that carry declarative request/gate constructs, which this core never needs. (3) The Bun test-file language gate is carried entirely by the realization (bunOnly, activation.facts[1]); tooling.languages keeps its production-source meaning. Stack membership (in Bun: test runner bun:test and the app serves htmx fragments) is realization data, so no new profile key is proposed and profileRequirements is empty — the obligation itself is fully neutral. The concrete forms of reaching the body (.text(), .json(), toContain, toMatch, markup assertion), the status/success assertion idioms, and the detector/validator ids (htmx_tester_detector) are realization details in bunOnly; the core states them generically as 'read the body, parse it, or match its content'. 'res.ok' is generalized to 'success flag'; the finding name status_asserted_body_never_reached names no stack and is kept in the neutral core. The legacy cross-reference coder.htmx.swap-oob-carries-id stays bunOnly. Severity 3 and the strict disposition are in core verification, not the profile, per the closed vocabulary.
